title: How Confidence Level Affects CI Width

steps.instruction: You'll build one bootstrap distribution, then read a confidence interval off it at **90%, then 95%, then 99%** confidence. **Before you start, commit to a prediction.**

gate.question: As you raise the confidence level from 90% → 95% → 99%, what happens to the width of the interval?

choices.text: It gets wider — more confidence needs a wider net
It gets narrower — more confidence means more precision
It stays the same — the confidence level doesn't affect width

gate.feedback: Higher confidence → **wider** interval. To be more sure you've captured the true value, you cast a wider net — the confidence-vs-precision trade-off. Now read the three intervals and see.
gate.retryFeedback: To be *more* confident you've captured the true value, do you need a wider or a narrower interval?

steps.observe: Note the **95% CI** bounds in the results panel. How wide is the interval?
steps.reveal: The 95% CI is roughly (9.7, 11.1) — a width of about 1.4 years.

steps.instruction: Change the confidence level dropdown to **90%**.
steps.observe: How did the interval change? Is it wider or narrower than the 95% CI?
steps.reveal: The 90% CI is narrower. We're accepting a higher chance of missing the true parameter (10% instead of 5%), so we don't need as wide a net.

steps.instruction: Now change the confidence level to **99%**.
steps.observe: Compare all three intervals. Which is widest? Which is narrowest?
steps.reveal: 99% is widest, 90% is narrowest. There's always a trade-off: **higher confidence = wider interval = less precision**. You can be very confident or very precise, but not both — unless you increase the sample size.

steps.instruction: You've compared 90%, 95%, and 99% confidence intervals. Put the key ideas in your own words.

prompts.label: What does "95% confident" mean, and why does 99% need to be wider than 95% to earn that extra confidence?
Is a headline reporting "5–50 mg/dL, 99% CI" useful? What trade-off did the researchers make?
How would the width of a 95% CI change with 4× as much data?

respond.answer: A strong answer: '95% confident' refers to the **method** — 95% of intervals built this way capture the true value; 99% must be wider because covering the truth more often needs a bigger net. A '5–50 mg/dL, 99% CI' is technically honest but nearly useless — they bought confidence at the cost of all precision. Quadrupling the data halves the width (width ∝ 1/√n), so 4× data → about half as wide.
